components.note: 氵 (water) — 泱 originally described a vast, flowing expanse of water, later extended to mean 'great, boundless' in general.
央 (yāng) gives the sound — an exact match with 泱's reading.

example.pinyin: Zhōngguó shì yí gè yāngyāng dà guó.
example.english: China is a vast and powerful nation.
example.fact: 泱泱大国 (yāngyāng dà guó) is a set phrase describing a nation of great size and long civilization — it is often used specifically to describe China's scale and history.

components.note: 走 (to walk, to go) — 趄 describes an unsteady, hesitant gait.
且 (qiě) no longer closely resembles 趄's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.pinyin: Tā yóuyù bù jué, jiǎobù zījū.
example.english: He couldn't make up his mind, and his steps were hesitant and unsteady.
example.fact: 趄 survives today almost only inside the two-character word 趑趄 (zījū), meaning to walk hesitantly or totter — one of many rare Chinese characters that exist only inside a single fixed compound.

components.note: 马 (horse) — 骅 names a type of fine, prized horse.
华 (huá) gives the sound — an exact match with 骅's reading.

example.pinyin: Gǔrén chēng jùnmǎ wéi huáliú.
example.english: Ancient people called fine horses 'hualiu.'
example.fact: 骅 appears almost only in the classical term 骅骝 (huáliú), a literary way of saying 'a superb horse' — 骝 alone names a horse with a black mane and tail on a reddish-brown body.

components.note: 阝 (here the 阜 radical, meaning 'mound, raised terrain') — 陲 relates to the physical edge of a territory.
垂 (chuí) gives the sound — an exact match with 陲's reading.

example.hanzi: 这座城市位于国家的边陲。
example.pinyin: Zhè zuò chéngshì wèiyú guójiā de biānchuí.
example.english: This city is located on the country's frontier.
example.fact: 陲 appears almost exclusively in 边陲 (biānchuí), meaning a remote border region — historically these frontier zones were often marked and defended using natural landforms like hills and ridges.

components.note: 阝 (here the 邑 radical, meaning 'settlement, place') — 郧 is used only as a place name.
员 (yuán) is close to the sound of 郧, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Yúnxī Xiàn wèiyú Húběi Shěng.
example.english: Yunxi County is located in Hubei Province.
example.fact: 郧 is used almost exclusively in place names, such as Yunxi County in Hubei — one of many Chinese characters whose entire modern use is confined to a single region's name.

meanings: used in 倜儻|倜傥[ti4 tang3]

components.note: 亻 (person) — 倜傥 describes a person's free, dashing manner.
周 (zhōu) may once have hinted at 倜's sound, but it no longer resembles the modern reading tì.

example.pinyin: Tā shì gè tìtǎng de niánqīng rén.
example.english: He is a dashing young man.
example.fact: 倜 appears almost only in 倜傥 (tìtǎng), a term for a free, dashing, debonair manner often used to describe romantic heroes in classical Chinese fiction and drama.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — marks the character as a phonetic transcription rather than a meaningful part, as is common for scientific loanwords and onomatopoeia.
令 (lìng) gives the sound — an exact match with 呤's reading.

example.hanzi: 嘌呤会在体内转化为尿酸。
example.pinyin: Piàolìng huì zài tǐnèi zhuǎnhuà wéi niàosuān.
example.english: Purines are converted into uric acid in the body.
example.fact: 嘌呤 (piàolìng) is the Chinese scientific term for 'purine,' a molecule found in DNA and RNA; when purines break down in the body they form uric acid, and too much uric acid causes gout.

components.note: 火 (fire) — 燧 names tools and signals used to make or carry fire.
遂 (suì) gives the sound — an exact match with 燧's reading.

example.hanzi: 古代士兵用烽燧传递消息。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài shìbīng yòng fēngsuì chuándì xiāoxi.
example.english: Ancient soldiers used beacon towers to relay messages.
example.fact: 烽燧 (fēngsuì) refers to the beacon-tower and smoke-signal system used along China's frontier defenses, including the Great Wall, to warn of approaching enemies.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 铉 names a metal tool.
玄 (xuán) is close to the sound of 铉 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.hanzi: 铉是古代抬鼎用的器具。
example.pinyin: Xuàn shì gǔdài tái dǐng yòng de qìjù.
example.english: 'Xuan' was the tool used in ancient times to carry a ceremonial tripod.
example.fact: In ancient China, the bronze ding (鼎) tripod cauldron was a symbol of state power used in rituals; 铉 named the carrying-bar used to lift one during ceremonies.

components.note: 米 (rice) — 粲 originally meant finely polished white rice; its brightness gave the character its extended sense of 'radiant, splendid.'

example.pinyin: Tā cànrán yíxiào.
example.english: She smiled radiantly.
example.fact: 粲 originally described finely polished white rice; the meaning extended metaphorically to 'bright, radiant,' as in 粲然一笑 (cànrán yíxiào), 'a radiant smile,' where gleaming teeth are likened to polished rice grains.

components.note: 骨 (bone) — 骶 names a bone at the base of the spine.
氐 (dǐ) gives the sound — an exact match with 骶's reading.

example.pinyin: Dǐgǔ zài jǐzhù de zuì xiàduān.
example.english: The sacrum is at the very bottom of the spine.
example.fact: 骶骨 (dǐgǔ), the sacrum, is the triangular bone formed by fused vertebrae at the base of the human spine, connecting it to the pelvis.

components.note: 山 (mountain) — 峁 names a rounded hill.
卯 (mǎo) gives the sound — an exact match with 峁's reading.

example.pinyin: Huángtǔ Gāoyuán shàng yǒu hěn duō mǎo.
example.english: There are many rounded loess hills on the Loess Plateau.
example.fact: 峁 (mǎo) is a geography term for the rounded hilltops typical of China's Loess Plateau, used alongside 塬 (a flat-topped plateau) and 沟 (a gully) to classify this heavily eroded landscape.

components.note: 忄 (heart, emotion) — 忸 describes the feeling of embarrassment.
丑 (chǒu) no longer closely resembles 忸's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.pinyin: Tā niǔní de xiào le.
example.english: She smiled bashfully.
example.fact: 忸 almost always appears in 忸怩 (niǔní), meaning bashful or embarrassed hesitation; both characters carry the 忄 (heart) radical, since Chinese groups emotion-related words under this component.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 渌 describes strained, clear water, and names a river.
录 (lù) gives the sound — an exact match with 渌's reading.

example.pinyin: Lù Shuǐ qīngchè jiàn dǐ.
example.english: The Lu River is clear all the way to the bottom.
example.fact: 渌 names the Lu River (渌水) in Hunan province, a tributary of the Xiang River — one of many obscure Chinese characters that survive today mainly as a river's proper name.

etymologyHint: A soldier 宀 mounting a horse 马

components.note: 马 (horse) — 骞 depicts a horse or rider rising up, giving the character its meaning 'to soar, hold high.'

example.pinyin: Zhāng Qiān kāitōng le Sīchóu zhī Lù.
example.english: Zhang Qian opened up the Silk Road.
example.fact: Zhang Qian (张骞) was a Han-dynasty imperial envoy whose westward journeys around 138 BCE opened diplomatic and trade contact with Central Asia, laying the groundwork for the Silk Road.

components.note: 髟 (hair) — 髭 names hair growing on the face.
此 (cǐ) is close to the sound of 髭, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Tā zuǐ shàng liú zhe zīxū.
example.english: He has a mustache on his lip.
example.fact: Traditional Chinese has separate words for different areas of facial hair: 髭 for the mustache above the lip, 须 for the chin beard, and 髯 for the cheek whiskers — a finer vocabulary distinction than English's single word 'beard.'

components.note: 戈 (spear, weapon) — 戡 means to subdue by force.
甚 (shén) no longer closely resembles 戡's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.pinyin: Zhèngfǔ pài jūnduì qù kānluàn.
example.english: The government sent the army to suppress the rebellion.
example.fact: 戡乱 (kānluàn, 'suppressing rebellion') names the 'Period of Mobilization for the Suppression of Communist Rebellion,' a state of emergency the Republic of China government in Taiwan maintained from 1948 until it was formally lifted in 1991.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 钨 names a metallic element.
乌 (wū) gives the sound — an exact match with 钨's reading.

example.pinyin: Wū de róngdiǎn fēicháng gāo.
example.english: Tungsten's melting point is extremely high.
example.fact: Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal, about 3,422°C (6,192°F) — the reason it was long used for light bulb filaments.

etymologyHint: A bright 矞 wit 讠; 矞 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 谲 describes speech or behavior that is cunning and deceitful.
矞 (yù) depicts a piercing brightness; paired with 讠 it suggests a dazzling but deceptive kind of talk. Its modern reading no longer resembles 谲's pronunciation jué.

example.pinyin: Guójì júshì guǐjué duōbiàn.
example.english: The international situation is strange and constantly changing.
example.fact: 谲 commonly appears in 诡谲 (guǐjué), meaning 'strange and unpredictable' — often used in the phrase 风云诡谲 to describe a volatile, hard-to-read situation.

components.note: 艹 (grass, plant) — 苋 names a leafy vegetable.
见 (jiàn) gives the sound — an exact match with 苋's reading.

example.pinyin: Māma chǎo le yì pán xiàncài.
example.english: Mom stir-fried a plate of amaranth greens.
example.fact: 苋菜 (xiàncài, amaranth greens), a common Chinese vegetable, turns its cooking water bright red or purple because of natural pigments in its leaves.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 锃 originally described metal polished to a shine.
呈 (chéng) is close to the sound of 锃, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Tā bǎ píxié cā de zèngliàng.
example.english: He polished his leather shoes until they gleamed.
example.fact: 锃 appears almost exclusively in 锃亮 (zèngliàng), describing something polished to a gleaming shine — most often shoes, metal, or floors in everyday Chinese speech.

components.note: 虫 (a small creature) — used broadly in Chinese for small animals, including shellfish like the clam.
利 (lì) is close to the sound of 蜊 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.pinyin: Wǒ xǐhuan chī gélí.
example.english: I like to eat clams.
example.fact: 蛤蜊 (gélí) is one of the most common words for 'clam' in Chinese cuisine, especially in coastal regions like Shandong and Fujian where clam dishes are a everyday staple.

etymologyHint: A room 屋 made of cloth 巾; 屋 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 巾 (cloth) — a tent is made of cloth.
屋 (wū, 'room') — depicts a shelter, echoing 幄's meaning of a tent; its reading is only loosely similar to 幄's wò.

example.pinyin: Tā shànyú yùnchóu wéiwò.
example.english: He is skilled at strategic planning from behind the scenes.
example.fact: 帷幄 (wéiwò), meaning a general's command tent, gives rise to the idiom 运筹帷幄 ('to strategize from within the command tent'), used today to praise skillful high-level planning.

components.note: 门 (door) — 闼 names a door or gate.
达 (dá) is close to the sound of 闼, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Tā tuī kāi mén tà, zǒu le jìnqù.
example.english: He pushed open the door and walked in.
example.fact: 闼 appears in the famous Song-dynasty poem line 两山排闼送青来 (Wang Anshi, 《书湖阴先生壁》), which imagines mountains 'pushing open the door' to send in their greenery.

components.note: 戈 (spear, weapon) — 戕 originally meant to kill or wound with a weapon.
爿 (qiáng) is close to the sound of 戕 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.pinyin: Xīyān huì qiānghài shēntǐ jiànkāng.
example.english: Smoking harms physical health.
example.fact: 戕 originally meant to kill or wound with a weapon; today it survives mainly in the literary compound 戕害 (qiānghài), meaning to harm or damage, often used for long-term harm to health or the environment.

components.note: 马 (horse) — 骊 originally described a pure black horse.
丽 (lì) gives the sound — an exact match with 骊's reading.

example.pinyin: Lí Shān fùjìn yǒu Qín Shǐhuáng Líng.
example.english: Near Mount Li is the mausoleum of Emperor Qin Shi Huang.
example.fact: 骊山 (Mount Li), near Xi'an, is where the Terracotta Army and the mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang, China's first emperor, are located — one of the most significant archaeological sites in the world.

meanings: name of ancient feudal State in Shenxi and Hunan

example.hanzi: “假途灭虢”是一个著名的历史计策。
example.pinyin: “Jiǎ tú miè Guó” shì yí gè zhùmíng de lìshǐ jìcè.
example.english: 'Borrowing a route to destroy Guo' is a famous historical stratagem.
example.fact: 假途灭虢 ('borrowing a route to destroy Guo') is one of the Thirty-Six Stratagems from ancient Chinese military strategy: using a request for passage as a pretext to conquer the state one is passing through, named after the real ancient state of 虢 (Guo).

meanings: to cook (rice etc) with vegetables, meat and water

components.note: 火 (fire) — 烩 names a cooking method using heat.
会 (huì) gives the sound — an exact match with 烩's reading.

example.hanzi: 他把所有的问题都一锅烩了。
example.pinyin: Tā bǎ suǒyǒu de wèntí dōu yìguōhuì le.
example.english: He lumped all the problems together into one pot.
example.fact: The idiom 一锅烩 (yìguōhuì), literally 'to braise everything in one pot,' criticizes treating very different things as if they were all the same, without proper distinction.

meanings: used in 倜儻|倜傥[ti4 tang3]

components.note: 亻 (person) — historically groups 傥 among person-related characters, though its meaning 'if, supposing' developed later as a grammatical usage.
党 (dǎng) is close to the sound of 傥, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 傥若明天下雨,我们就不去了。
example.pinyin: Tǎngruò míngtiān xiàyǔ, wǒmen jiù bú qù le.
example.english: If it rains tomorrow, we won't go.
example.fact: 傥 is a literary variant of 倘 (tǎng, 'if'); today it survives mainly in classical texts and in the compound 倜傥 (tìtǎng), describing a free and dashing manner.

meanings: concubine of last ruler of the Shang dynasty

components.note: 女 (woman) — 妲 is used only as part of a woman's name.
旦 (dàn) is close to the sound of 妲, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 妲己是商朝的著名王妃。
example.pinyin: Dájǐ shì Shāngcháo de zhùmíng wángfēi.
example.english: Daji was a famous royal consort of the Shang dynasty.
example.fact: 妲己 (Daji) is a legendary consort of King Zhou, the last ruler of the Shang dynasty, traditionally blamed for his downfall — she remains a major character in Chinese folklore and the classic novel Investiture of the Gods.

components.note: 纟 (silk, thread) — 绌 originally related to sewing, and came to mean falling short or being deficient.
出 (chū) is close to the sound of 绌 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.hanzi: 和他比起来,我相形见绌。
example.pinyin: Hé tā bǐ qǐlái, wǒ xiāngxíng jiànchù.
example.english: Compared to him, I pale in comparison.
example.fact: 绌 appears mainly in the common idiom 相形见绌 (xiāngxíng jiànchù), meaning 'to be shown up by comparison,' used when something looks inferior next to something else.

meanings: the forking branch of a tree

components.note: 木 (tree, wood) — 桠 names a part of a tree.
亚 (yà) is close to the sound of 桠 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.pinyin: Nà kē shù de yāzhī hěn màomì.
example.english: That tree's forking branches are very dense.
example.fact: 桠 specifically names the point where a tree branch forks into two — a level of botanical precision that English usually just calls 'a fork in the branch.'

components.note: 衣 (clothes) — 袈 names a garment.
加 (jiā) gives the sound — an exact match with 袈's reading.

example.pinyin: Héshang chuānzhe jiāshā.
example.english: The monk is wearing a Buddhist robe.
example.fact: 袈裟 (jiāshā), the patchwork outer robe worn by Buddhist monks, is a Chinese transliteration of the Sanskrit word 'kashaya' — one of many Buddhist terms that entered Chinese as a sound loanword rather than a translated meaning.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 鎗, like 枪, names a metal weapon.
仓 (cāng) is part of a phonetic family that gives several characters (枪, 抢, 戗, 呛) a similar 'qiang'-family sound; it shares 鎗's final -ang but not its initial.

example.pinyin: Shìbīng shǒuchí qiāngzhī.
example.english: The soldier held a rifle in hand.
example.fact: 鎗 is an old variant form of 枪 (qiāng, 'gun'); both share the component 仓, part of a family of characters — 枪, 戗, 呛, 跄 — that all carry a related 'qiang' sound from the same root.

components.note: 艹 (grass) — 薮 originally named a marsh thick with vegetation.
数 (shù) no longer closely resembles 薮's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.pinyin: Zhèlǐ céng shì tǔfěi de yuānsǒu.
example.english: This place was once a den of bandits.
example.fact: 薮 originally named a marsh where plants and animals gathered; by extension, 渊薮 (yuānsǒu) came to mean any place where people or things of a certain kind congregate, like a 'den' or 'haunt.'

meanings: to press (with one's hand or finger)

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 揿 means to press with the hand.
钦 (qīn) is close to the sound of 揿 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.pinyin: Tā qìn le yíxià ménlíng.
example.english: She pressed the doorbell.
example.fact: 揿 is common in southern Chinese dialects, such as Shanghainese, for 'to press'; the compound 揿钮 (qìnniǔ) specifically means a snap fastener used on clothing.

etymologyHint: The sun 日 rising over the woods 木

components.note: 日 (sun) — placed above the trees, it depicts the sun rising.
木 (tree, woods) — the sun 日 rising above the treeline suggests bright morning light.

example.pinyin: “Shījīng” zhōng yǒu “gǎogǎo chū rì” de shījù.
example.english: The Book of Songs contains the line 'gaogao chu ri' (the brilliant sun emerges).
example.fact: 杲杲出日 ('the brilliant sun rises') is a line from the Book of Songs (诗经), China's oldest poetry collection; 杲 depicts the sun 日 rising above the trees 木, visually suggesting brightness.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh, body) — 肓 names a region of the body.
亡 (wáng) no longer closely resembles 肓's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 他的病已经病入膏肓了。
example.pinyin: Tā de bìng yǐjīng bìngrù gāohuāng le.
example.english: His illness has already become incurable.
example.fact: 病入膏肓 (bìngrù gāohuāng) is a well-known idiom meaning a situation is beyond remedy; it comes from ancient Chinese medicine, where 膏 and 肓 named two areas near the heart considered impossible for a doctor's needle or medicine to reach.

etymologyHint: A building 厂 containing the past 昔

components.note: 厂 (a simple shelter or building) — ties to 厝's meaning of a dwelling.
昔 (the past, formerly) — suggests a structure that has stood since a former time.

example.hanzi: 在福建,“厝”是“房子”的意思。
example.pinyin: Zài Fújiàn, “cuò” shì “fángzi” de yìsi.
example.english: In Fujian, 'cuo' means 'house.'
example.fact: In Southern Min (Hokkien) dialect regions like Fujian and Taiwan, 厝 means 'house' and appears widely in place names, such as a neighborhood named after its founding family.

meanings: variant of 蒞|莅[li4], to attend
etymologyHint: A place 位 where grass 艹 grows; 立 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 艹 (grass) — ties 莅 to its component parts, though the meaning 'to attend' developed through sound-borrowing rather than this image.
位 (position, place) — contains 立, whose reading lì matches 莅's reading exactly.

example.hanzi: 我们诚挚邀请您莅临本次活动。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen chéngzhì yāoqǐng nín lìlín běn cì huódòng.
example.english: We sincerely invite you to attend this event.
example.fact: 莅临 (lìlín) is standard formal Chinese for 'to be present' or 'to attend,' used constantly on invitation cards, banners, and opening-ceremony announcements.

meanings: used in 氤氳|氤氲[yin1 yun1]

components.note: 气 (gas, vapor) — 氤 describes mist and vapor.
因 (yīn) gives the sound — an exact match with 氤's reading.

example.pinyin: Shānjiān wùqì yīnyūn.
example.english: Mist swirls hazily among the mountains.
example.fact: 氤氲 (yīnyūn) is a classical Chinese term for swirling mist or vapor, often used in poetry to evoke a hazy, dreamlike atmosphere, such as incense smoke curling upward or fog drifting through mountains.

components.note: 纟 (silk) — 缙 originally described a shade of red silk.
晋 (jìn) gives the sound — an exact match with 缙's reading.

example.hanzi: 缙云山是重庆有名的风景区。
example.pinyin: Jìnyún Shān shì Chóngqìng yǒumíng de fēngjǐng qū.
example.english: Jinyun Mountain is a famous scenic area in Chongqing.
example.fact: 缙云山, near Chongqing, is a national nature reserve known for its rich subtropical forest and Buddhist temples — one of the few places 缙 survives in everyday use, inside a proper name.

meanings: ceremonial dress worn by the emperor
etymologyHint: A duke 公 in his robes 衣

components.note: 公 (a duke, lord) — 衮 names a nobleman's ceremonial dress.
衣 (clothes) — 衮 is a type of formal robe.

example.pinyin: Huángdì chuānzhe gǔnfú jì tiān.
example.english: The emperor wore his ceremonial robe to perform the rites to heaven.
example.fact: 衮服 (gǔnfú) was the formal ceremonial robe worn by Chinese emperors for state rituals such as sacrifices to heaven, richly embroidered with dragons and other imperial symbols.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 诟 means to abuse or revile with words.
后 (hòu) is close to the sound of 诟, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 这部电影的剧情备受诟病。
example.pinyin: Zhè bù diànyǐng de jùqíng bèishòu gòubìng.
example.english: This movie's plot has been widely criticized.
example.fact: 诟病 (gòubìng) is a common modern phrase meaning 'widely criticized' or 'a flaw that draws criticism,' frequently seen in Chinese news and reviews, as in 备受诟病 ('widely condemned').

components.note: 方 (here derived from a flag/banner form) — ties 旖 to soft, fluttering movement, echoed in its meaning 'gentle, charming.'
奇 (qí) is close to the sound of 旖, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Nàlǐ de fēngguāng yǐnǐ.
example.english: The scenery there is gorgeous and charming.
example.fact: 旖旎 (yǐnǐ) is a poetic term almost always used to describe soft, beautiful scenery, as in the common phrase 风光旖旎 ('gorgeous scenery'), frequently seen in Chinese travel writing.

components.note: 石 (mineral, stone) — 硒 names a chemical element.
西 (xī) gives the sound — an exact match with 硒's reading.

example.pinyin: Bāxī jiānguǒ fùhán xī yuánsù.
example.english: Brazil nuts are rich in selenium.
example.fact: Brazil nuts are one of the richest natural sources of selenium, an essential trace mineral — just one or two nuts can provide an adult's entire recommended daily intake.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 唁 is a speech act, expressing condolence.
言 (yán) is close to the sound of 唁 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.pinyin: Gèguó lǐngdǎorén fā lái yàndiàn.
example.english: Leaders from various countries sent messages of condolence.
example.fact: 唁电 (yàndiàn), a formal telegram or message of condolence, is a standard term in Chinese diplomatic and news reporting whenever a head of state or notable figure passes away.

components.note: 女 (woman) — historically groups 嬗 among characters relating to lineage and succession.
亶 (dǎn) is close to the sound of 嬗, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Shèhuì guānniàn zài búduàn shànbiàn.
example.english: Social attitudes are constantly evolving.
example.fact: 嬗变 (shànbiàn) describes a gradual, often profound transformation — used both in the humanities, for cultural or social change, and in physics, where it also denotes nuclear transmutation.

components.note: 石 (stone) — 硎 names a sharpening stone.
刑 (xíng) gives the sound — an exact match with 硎's reading.

example.hanzi: 庄子说刀刃“若新发于硎”。
example.pinyin: Zhuāngzǐ shuō dāorèn “ruò xīn fā yú xíng”.
example.english: Zhuangzi said the blade's edge was 'as if freshly sharpened on a whetstone.'
example.fact: The phrase comes from Zhuangzi's famous 'Butcher Ding' parable, where after nineteen years of use, the butcher's knife remains 'as if freshly sharpened on a whetstone' (硎) — a metaphor for mastering a skill so well it causes no wear at all.

meanings: to mount maps or scrolls to paste
etymologyHint: To display 表 a cloth 衤 map; 表 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 衤 (cloth) — mounting a painting involves backing it with cloth or paper.
表 (biǎo) matches 裱's reading exactly, and also means 'to display, show' — fitting for mounting a work of art for display.

example.pinyin: Shīfu zhèngzài biǎo yì fú huà.
example.english: The craftsman is mounting a painting.
example.fact: 裱画 (biǎohuà), the traditional Chinese craft of mounting paintings and calligraphy onto silk or paper scrolls, is essential to preserving and displaying these artworks — a specialized profession still practiced today.

components.note: 卑 (to despise, look down on) — frowning is the facial expression of contempt or displeasure.
频 (pín) gives the sound — an exact match with 颦's reading.

example.hanzi: 《红楼梦》里,林黛玉有个外号叫“颦儿”。
example.pinyin: “Hónglóumèng” lǐ, Lín Dàiyù yǒu gè wàihào jiào “Pín'ér”.
example.english: In 'Dream of the Red Chamber,' Lin Daiyu has a nickname, 'Pin'er.'
example.fact: In the classic novel Dream of the Red Chamber, Jia Baoyu nicknames Lin Daiyu '颦儿' (Pin'er) because of her characteristically knitted brows (颦) — a detail meant to suggest her delicate, melancholic beauty.

components.note: 貝 (贝, shell — ancient currency) — 質 relates to material value and substance.
斦 (an ancient component rarely used on its own) no longer resembles 質's modern reading zhì — the connection has been lost over time.

example.pinyin: “Zhì” shì “zhì” de fántǐzì.
example.english: 'Zhi' (質) is the traditional character form of 'zhi' (质).
example.fact: 質 is the traditional form of 质 (zhì), a character used constantly in words like 质量 (zhìliàng, 'quality'); mainland China's character simplification in the 1950s streamlined its top portion into the simpler form seen in 质 today.

components.note: 面 (face) — 靥 names a feature of the face.
厌 (yàn) is close to the sound of 靥, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Tā xiào qǐlái yǒu yí duì jiǔyè.
example.english: When she smiles, she has a pair of dimples.
example.fact: 酒靥 (jiǔyè), literally 'wine dimples,' is a classical Chinese term for dimples — named for the little hollows that a cup of wine might rest in, a fanciful image from old poetry.

components.note: 乞 (to beg) — historically groups 纥 among characters written with this shape, though the link to its meaning 'inferior silk' is not transparent today.
纟 (sī) no longer closely resembles 纥's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 回纥是唐朝时期的一个民族。
example.pinyin: Huígē shì Tángcháo shíqī de yí gè mínzú.
example.english: The Huige were a people of the Tang dynasty period.
example.fact: 纥 appears in 回纥 (Huígē), the Tang-dynasty Chinese name for the Uyghur people's ancestors, who founded a powerful steppe empire allied with and later at odds with the Tang court.

components.note: 火 (fire) — 煨 means to cook slowly over gentle heat.
畏 (wèi) is close to the sound of 煨 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.pinyin: Nǎinai yòng xiǎo huǒ wēi tāng.
example.english: Grandma simmers soup over a low flame.
example.fact: 煨 describes cooking slowly at a low, gentle heat, often in embers or ash in traditional cooking — a technique still used for soups and stews that need many hours to develop flavor.

meanings: used in 磅礡|磅礴[pang2 bo2]

components.note: 石 (stone) — 礴 describes something as vast and imposing as stone.
薄 (bó) gives the sound — an exact match with 礴's reading.

example.pinyin: Zhè fú huà qìshì pángbó.
example.english: This painting has a grand, sweeping power.
example.fact: 礴 exists only in the compound 磅礴 (pángbó), describing something of vast, sweeping power or grandeur — often used for mountains, oceans, or ambitious works of art.

components.note: 金 (metal) — 鏖 relates to metal weapons used in fierce battle.
鹿 (lù) no longer closely resembles 鏖's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.pinyin: Liǎng jūn áozhàn le sān tiān sān yè.
example.english: The two armies fought a fierce, prolonged battle for three days and three nights.
example.fact: 鏖战 (áozhàn) describes a long, grueling battle fought to exhaustion — the word is still commonly used today outside of warfare, for sports matches or competitions that drag on fiercely.

meanings: see 蟈蟈|蝈蝈 long-horned grasshopper

components.note: 虫 (insect) — 蝈 names an insect.
国 (guó) is close to the sound of 蝈 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.hanzi: 夏天能听到蝈蝈的叫声。
example.pinyin: Xiàtiān néng tīng dào guōguo de jiào shēng.
example.english: In summer you can hear the chirping of katydids.
example.fact: 蝈蝈 (guōguo) is the Chinese name for a katydid, a loud-chirping green insect traditionally kept by hobbyists in small woven cages to enjoy its song, much like a cricket.

meanings: tablet held by someone having authority

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — 笏 was traditionally made of bamboo, jade, or ivory.
勿 (wù) is close to the sound of 笏, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 古代官员上朝时手持笏板。
example.pinyin: Gǔdài guānyuán shàngcháo shí shǒuchí hùbǎn.
example.english: Ancient officials held a ceremonial tablet in hand when attending court.
example.fact: 笏 (hù) was a narrow ceremonial tablet that imperial officials held while addressing the emperor at court, originally used to jot notes and later kept mainly as a mark of rank.

etymologyHint: A man drawing 廾 an arrow 羽

components.note: 羽 (feather) — evokes the feathered shaft of an arrow.
廾 (two hands together) — depicts hands drawing back a bow.

example.pinyin: Hòu Yì shè xià le jiǔ gè tàiyáng.
example.english: Hou Yi shot down nine suns.
example.fact: In Chinese mythology, the archer Hou Yi (后羿) shot down nine of ten suns that were scorching the earth, leaving just one — he is also known as the husband of Chang'e, the moon goddess celebrated at the Mid-Autumn Festival.

components.note: 鼎 (a ritual bronze tripod) — 鼐 names a large ceremonial vessel.
乃 (nǎi) is close to the sound of 鼐 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.hanzi: 鼐是古代用来烧香的大鼎。
example.pinyin: Nài shì gǔdài yòng lái shāo xiāng de dà dǐng.
example.english: A 'nai' was a large ancient tripod used for burning incense.
example.fact: 鼐 names a large ding (鼎), the bronze ritual tripod cauldron that was one of the most important symbols of political and religious authority in ancient China.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 湟 names a river.
皇 (huáng) gives the sound — an exact match with 湟's reading.

example.hanzi: 湟水是黄河的一条支流。
example.pinyin: Huáng Shuǐ shì Huáng Hé de yì tiáo zhīliú.
example.english: The Huang River is a tributary of the Yellow River.
example.fact: 湟水 (the Huang River), which flows through Qinghai province, is a major tributary of the Yellow River and gives its name to Xining's historic Hehuang region.

components.note: 瓦 (pottery, tile) — 甑 names an earthenware cooking vessel.
曾 (zēng) is close to the sound of 甑 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.pinyin: Gǔrén yòng zèng zhēng fàn.
example.english: Ancient people used a zeng to steam rice.
example.fact: 甑 (zèng) was an ancient earthenware or bronze pot with a perforated bottom, set above a boiling pot of water to steam rice — one of the earliest known steaming vessels in Chinese cooking, dating back thousands of years.

components.note: 火 (fire) — 炜 describes a bright, glowing red.
韦 (wéi) is close to the sound of 炜 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.pinyin: Xīyáng bǎ tiānkōng rǎn de wěihóng.
example.english: The setting sun dyed the sky a glowing red.
example.fact: 炜 describes a bright, glowing red or brilliant light; today it survives mainly as a character chosen for personal given names, valued for its bright, warm meaning.

meanings: to cook slowly in such a pot

components.note: 火 (fire) — 煲 means to cook slowly with heat.
保 (bǎo) is close to the sound of 煲 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.pinyin: Guǎngdōng rén xǐhuan bāo tāng.
example.english: Cantonese people love to slow-cook soup.
example.fact: 煲汤 (bāo tāng), slow-simmered soup, is a signature part of Cantonese cuisine, often cooked for hours with meat, herbs, and dried ingredients believed to have health benefits.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 锉 names a metal tool.
坐 (zuò) is close to the sound of 锉, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Tā yòng cuòdāo bǎ mùtou mó píng.
example.english: He used a file to smooth down the wood.
example.fact: 锉刀 (cuòdāo), a metal file, is a basic hand tool used to grind and smooth the surface of wood, metal, or plastic by rubbing its ridged surface back and forth.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — 笕 names a pipe made of bamboo.
见 (jiàn) is close to the sound of 笕, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 山泉水通过笕流进院子。
example.pinyin: Shānquán shuǐ tōngguò jiǎn liú jìn yuànzi.
example.english: Mountain spring water flows into the courtyard through a bamboo pipe.
example.fact: 笕 (jiǎn) named a length of hollowed bamboo used to channel water from a spring, a simple gravity-fed piping system still echoed today in ornamental bamboo water fountains.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 喑 relates to being unable to speak.
音 (yīn) gives the sound — an exact match with 喑's reading.

example.hanzi: 他气得说不出话,如喑一般。
example.pinyin: Tā qì de shuō bu chū huà, rú yīn yìbān.
example.english: He was so angry he couldn't speak, as if struck mute.
example.fact: 喑 describes being struck mute or unable to speak; the compound 万马齐喑 ('ten thousand horses all struck silent'), from a poem by Qing-dynasty writer Gong Zizhen, describes a society too repressed to voice dissent.

components.note: 山 (mountain) — 嶂 names a steep mountain barrier.
章 (zhāng) is close to the sound of 嶂 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.pinyin: Yuǎnchù qúnshān céngluán diézhàng.
example.english: In the distance, mountain ranges rise in overlapping peaks.
example.fact: 层峦叠嶂 (céngluán diézhàng), 'layered peaks and stacked ridges,' is a common four-character phrase in Chinese landscape description and painting, evoking mountains receding in overlapping layers.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 浔 names a riverbank.
寻 (xún) gives the sound — an exact match with 浔's reading.

example.pinyin: Jiǔjiāng gǔ chēng Xúnyáng.
example.english: Jiujiang was anciently called Xunyang.
example.fact: 浔阳 (Xunyang) was the historical name of Jiujiang, a city on the Yangtze River in Jiangxi province — the setting of Bai Juyi's famous Tang-dynasty poem 'The Song of the Pipa' (琵琶行).

components.note: 弓 (bow) — 弭 originally named a type of bow; the character was later used to mean 'to stop, calm, quell,' as in 消弭.

example.pinyin: Shuāngfāng nǔlì xiāomǐ máodùn.
example.english: Both sides worked hard to eliminate the conflict.
example.fact: 弭 survives mainly in 消弭 (xiāomǐ), meaning 'to eliminate or dispel' a conflict, threat, or disaster — a formal word common in news and diplomatic language.

etymologyHint: A woman 女 watching over her ward 区

components.note: 女 (woman) — 妪 names an old woman.
区 (an enclosed area, ward) — suggests a woman keeping watch over those in her care.

example.pinyin: Lǎoyù zuò zài ménkǒu shài tàiyáng.
example.english: The old woman sat at the door sunbathing.
example.fact: 妪 appears mainly in the literary term 老妪 (lǎoyù, 'an old woman') — a word that survives today mostly in written Chinese, since everyday speech prefers 老太太 or 老奶奶.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 锂 names a metallic element.
里 (lǐ) gives the sound — an exact match with 锂's reading.

example.pinyin: Shǒujī diànchí hányǒu lǐ.
example.english: Cell phone batteries contain lithium.
example.fact: Lithium is the lightest of all metals and is the key ingredient in lithium-ion batteries, which power most smartphones, laptops, and electric vehicles today.

components.note: 艹 (grass, plant) — 苡 names a grain plant.
以 (yǐ) gives the sound — an exact match with 苡's reading.

example.pinyin: Yìmǐ chángyòng lái zhǔ zhōu.
example.english: Job's tears are often used to make congee.
example.fact: 薏米 (yìmǐ, 'Job's tears'), whose name contains 苡, is a grain widely used in Chinese cooking and traditional medicine, especially in congee.

components.note: 子 (child) — 孳 relates to breeding and reproduction.
兹 (zī) gives the sound — an exact match with 孳's reading.

example.hanzi: 潮湿的环境容易孳生细菌。
example.pinyin: Cháoshī de huánjìng róngyì zīshēng xìjūn.
example.english: A damp environment easily breeds bacteria.
example.fact: 孳生 (zīshēng) is the standard Chinese term for organisms breeding or multiplying, commonly used in public-health warnings about bacteria, mosquitoes, or other pests thriving in damp conditions.

components.note: 页 (head) — 颏 names a part of the face.
亥 (hài) no longer closely resembles 颏's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.pinyin: Tā yǒudiǎn shuāng xiàké.
example.english: He has a bit of a double chin.
example.fact: 颏 means 'chin' and is the character behind 下颏 (xiàké), the everyday word for the chin; in ornithology it also names the throat patch used to describe and identify bird species.

components.note: 酉 (wine) — 醴 names a sweet wine.
豊 (lǐ) gives the sound — an exact match with 醴's reading.

example.pinyin: Líling shì zhùmíng de cídū.
example.english: Liling is a famous porcelain capital.
example.fact: 醴陵, a city in Hunan province, is one of China's major porcelain-producing centers, often called a 'porcelain capital' alongside Jingdezhen.

etymologyHint: The sun 日 shining through a doorway 門

components.note: 門 (door, gate) — a doorway that light can shine through.
日 (sun) — sunlight passing through the doorway visually suggests a gap, or the space 'between' two things.

example.pinyin: “Jiān” shì “jiān” de fántǐzì.
example.english: 'Jian' (間) is the traditional form of 'jian' (间).
example.fact: 間 depicts the sun 日 shining through a doorway 門 — visually representing the gap or space 'between' two things, the core meaning behind words like 中间 (zhōngjiān, 'in the middle').

components.note: 氵 (water) — 渚 names a small sandbank in a river.
者 (zhě) is close to the sound of 渚, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 杜甫写道:“渚清沙白鸟飞回。”
example.pinyin: Dù Fǔ xiědào: “Zhǔ qīng shā bái niǎo fēi huí.”
example.english: Du Fu wrote: 'The islet is clear, the sand is white, birds fly back.'
example.fact: This line opens Du Fu's Tang-dynasty poem 登高 ('Climbing High'), widely regarded as one of the greatest classical Chinese poems ever written; 渚 refers to a small sandbank or islet in a river.

components.note: 车 (cart) — 轭 names a part of a cart's harness.
厄 (è) gives the sound — an exact match with 轭's reading.

example.pinyin: Nóngfū gěi niú tào shàng è.
example.english: The farmer put a yoke on the ox.
example.fact: 轭 (è) names the wooden crossbar fitted across an ox's or horse's neck so it can pull a cart or plow — one of the oldest agricultural tools in continuous use.

components.note: 鸟 (bird) — 鹬 names a shorebird.
矞 (yù) gives the sound — an exact match with 鹬's reading.

example.hanzi: “鹬蚌相争,渔翁得利”是一个著名的成语。
example.pinyin: “Yù bàng xiāng zhēng, yúwēng dé lì” shì yí gè zhùmíng de chéngyǔ.
example.english: 'When the snipe and the clam fight, the fisherman profits' is a famous idiom.
example.fact: The idiom tells of a snipe (鹬) and a clam locked in a fight, neither willing to let go, until a fisherman simply picks up both — a warning that rivals who refuse to compromise let a third party profit from their conflict.

etymologyHint: A hairy 毛 worm 虫; 毛 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 虫 (a small creature) — used broadly in Chinese for small animals, including shellfish like the oyster.
毛 (máo, 'hair, fur') — its shaggy image may allude to the oyster's rough shell; the reading is only loosely close to 蚝's háo.

example.pinyin: Zhōngcān jīngcháng yòng háoyóu tiáowèi.
example.english: Chinese cooking often uses oyster sauce for flavoring.
example.fact: 蚝油 (háoyóu, oyster sauce), made from oyster extracts, is one of the most widely used condiments in Cantonese and broader Chinese cooking.

example.hanzi: 黃是“黄”的本字,意思是黄色。
example.pinyin: Huáng shì “huáng” de běnzì, yìsi shì huángsè.
example.english: Huang (黃) is the original form of huang (黄), meaning 'yellow.'
example.fact: 黃/黄 is also one of the most common Chinese surnames, and traditionally the color yellow was associated with the earth and with the legendary Yellow Emperor (黄帝), considered an ancestor of the Chinese people.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh) — 膘 names body fat.
票 (piào) is close to the sound of 膘, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Dōngtiān zhū róngyì zhǎng biāo.
example.english: In winter, pigs easily gain fat.
example.fact: 长膘 (zhǎng biāo) is a common colloquial term for gaining weight or fat — originally used for livestock being fattened, and now often used humorously for people too.

components.note: 阝 (here the 阜 radical, 'mound') — 邛 relates to raised land and place names.
工 (gōng) no longer closely resembles 邛's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 邛崃是四川的一座城市。
example.pinyin: Qiónglái shì Sìchuān de yí zuò chéngshì.
example.english: Qionglai is a city in Sichuan.
example.fact: 邛崃 (Qionglai), a city in Sichuan province, sits along the route of the ancient Southern Silk Road and is known today for its liquor-brewing industry.

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — 痨 names a disease.
劳 (láo) gives the sound — an exact match with 痨's reading.

example.hanzi: 过去人们把肺结核叫做“肺痨”。
example.pinyin: Guòqù rénmen bǎ fèijiéhé jiàozuò “fèiláo”.
example.english: In the past, people called tuberculosis 'fei lao.'
example.fact: 肺痨 (fèiláo) was the traditional Chinese name for tuberculosis before the modern medical term 肺结核 became standard — before antibiotics, it was one of the most feared and deadly diseases worldwide.

components.note: 衤 (clothes) — 褡 names an item of clothing.
荅 (dá) gives the sound — an exact match with 褡's reading.

example.pinyin: Tā bēizhe yí gè dālian.
example.english: He carried a traditional cloth pouch on his back.
example.fact: 褡裢 (dālian) was a traditional long, narrow cloth bag worn slung over the shoulder or waist, historically used by travelers and peddlers to carry money and small goods.

components.note: 耒 (a plow) — 耦 originally described two farmers plowing side by side.
禺 (yú) gives the sound — an exact match with 耦's reading.

example.hanzi: 配偶一词与“耦”的本义有关。
example.pinyin: Pèi'ǒu yìcí yǔ “ǒu” de běnyì yǒuguān.
example.english: The word for 'spouse' is related to the original meaning of 'ou.'
example.fact: 耦 originally described two farmers plowing side by side as a working pair; this sense of 'paired, matched' survives today in 配偶 (pèi'ǒu, 'spouse'), though modern Chinese usually writes that 'ǒu' with the person radical, as 偶, instead.

etymologyHint: From the east 早 to the west 覀

components.note: 覀 (west) — one edge of the extensive reach described by 覃.
早 (early, morning) — paired with 覀, suggests reaching from one end to the other.

example.pinyin: Tán shì Guǎngxī chángjiàn de xìngshì.
example.english: Tan is a common surname in Guangxi.
example.fact: 覃 (as a surname, pronounced Tán) is especially common in Guangxi, particularly among the Zhuang ethnic minority — one of many Chinese surnames tied strongly to a specific region and ethnic group.

etymologyHint: A tiger 虍 stalking in the bushes 丱

components.note: 虍 (tiger) — the top of 虛 depicts a tiger.
丱 (bushes, undergrowth) — a tiger lurking in the underbrush hints at the empty space around it.

example.pinyin: “Xūnǐ” de “xū” shì “xū” de fántǐzì.
example.english: The 'xu' in 'xuni' is the traditional form of 'xu.'
example.fact: 虛 is the traditional form of 虚 (xū, 'empty, false, virtual'), the character behind 虚拟现实 (xūnǐ xiànshí), the Chinese term for 'virtual reality.'

components.note: 饣 (food) — 馔 means food or a meal.
巽 (xùn) no longer closely resembles 馔's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.pinyin: Zhuō shàng bǎi mǎn le jiāyáo měizhuàn.
example.english: The table was full of delicious dishes.
example.fact: 馔 is a formal, literary word for food or a meal, typically found in phrases like 佳肴美馔 ('delicious delicacies') rather than in everyday conversation.

etymologyHint: A framework 罒 made of bamboo ⺮

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — 篾 names thin strips split from bamboo.

example.pinyin: Zhúmiè kěyǐ yòng lái biān lánzi.
example.english: Bamboo strips can be used to weave baskets.
example.fact: 竹篾 (zhúmiè), thin strips split from bamboo stalks, are the traditional raw material for weaving baskets, mats, and other everyday items across southern China.

example.pinyin: Yǎnzhōu shì gǔdài jiǔzhōu zhī yī.
example.english: Yanzhou was one of the Nine Provinces of ancient China.
example.fact: 兖州 (Yanzhou) was one of the legendary Nine Provinces (九州) described in the ancient text 禹贡 (Tribute of Yu); the name survives today as a district of Jining city in Shandong province.

components.note: 门 (gate) — 阋 describes conflict happening within the household, 'inside the gate.'
兒 (ér) no longer closely resembles 阋's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.pinyin: “Xiōngdì xìqiáng” bǐyù nèibù fēnzhēng.
example.english: 'Brothers fighting within the walls' is a metaphor for internal conflict.
example.fact: 兄弟阋墙 comes from the Book of Songs and describes internal strife within a family or group; the same poem adds 外御其侮 ('but uniting against outside insults'), contrasting internal conflict with external solidarity.

meanings: to make an excursion; to ramble; to travel
etymologyHint: To walk 辶 about 敖; 敖 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 辶 (to walk, move) — 遨 means to travel or roam freely.
敖 (áo) gives the exact same sound as 遨, and also carries a related sense of wandering freely.

example.hanzi: 中国航天员在太空遨游。
example.pinyin: Zhōngguó hángtiānyuán zài tàikōng áoyóu.
example.english: Chinese astronauts roam through space.
example.fact: The phrase 遨游太空 (áoyóu tàikōng, 'to roam through space') is commonly used in Chinese media to describe astronauts' spaceflights, giving the ancient word 遨 a modern, high-tech usage.

example.pinyin: “Yuán” zài gǔ Hànyǔ zhōng yìwéi “yúshì”.
example.english: 'Yuan,' in classical Chinese, means 'thereupon.'
example.fact: 爰 is a classical Chinese particle meaning 'thereupon, then,' common in ancient texts like the Book of Songs; it also serves as the phonetic component in 援 (yuán, 'to aid, pull'), where it keeps the exact same reading.

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — 痂 names a healing mark left by an injury.
加 (jiā) gives the sound — an exact match with 痂's reading.

example.pinyin: Shāngkǒu jié jiā le.
example.english: The wound has scabbed over.
example.fact: A scab (痂) forms when platelets and clotting proteins in the blood dry and harden over a wound, creating a protective barrier that lets new skin grow underneath.

components.note: 舟 (boat) — 艄 names a part of a boat.
肖 (xiào) no longer closely resembles 艄's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.pinyin: Shāogōng yáozhe chuán jiǎng.
example.english: The boatman rows the oar.
example.fact: 艄公 (shāogōng) is a traditional term for a boatman who steers from a vessel's stern (艄) — common in depictions of old river and canal life in China, such as along the Grand Canal.

components.note: 耒 (a plow) — 耨 means to hoe or weed with a farm tool.
辱 (rù) no longer closely resembles 耨's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.pinyin: Nóngmín gēngnòu tiándì.
example.english: Farmers plow and hoe the fields.
example.fact: 耨 is a classical word for hoeing or weeding; paired with 耕 ('to plow') in 耕耨, it represents the two most basic tasks of farming described in classical Chinese texts.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 沤 means to soak or steep in water.
区 (ōu) gives the sound — an exact match with 沤's reading.

example.pinyin: Nóngmín bǎ zácǎo ōuféi.
example.english: Farmers compost weeds into fertilizer by soaking and fermenting them.
example.fact: 沤肥 (ōuféi) is a traditional Chinese farming technique of soaking and fermenting plant waste and manure in water to break it down into fertilizer — a precursor to modern composting.

components.note: 辶 (to walk, move) — its precise link to 邋's meaning 'sloppy, ragged' is unclear; the character survives almost solely in the fixed compound 邋遢.
巤 (liè) is close to the sound of 邋, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Tā chuān de hěn lāta.
example.english: He dresses very sloppily.
example.fact: 邋遢 (lāta) is a common colloquial word for being sloppy, messy, or slovenly — 邋 essentially never appears anywhere except inside this one compound.

meanings: the sound of a fiercely-burning fire

components.note: 火 (fire) — 焓 relates to heat energy.
含 (hán) gives the sound — an exact match with 焓's reading.

example.hanzi: 物理学中,焓表示系统的热量。
example.pinyin: Wùlǐxué zhōng, hán biǎoshì xìtǒng de rèliàng.
example.english: In physics, enthalpy represents a system's heat content.
example.fact: 焓 (hán) is the Chinese scientific term for 'enthalpy,' a thermodynamic measure of a system's total heat content, essential in chemistry and engineering calculations involving energy.

components.note: 禾 (grain) — 秣 names grain fed to animals.
末 (mò) gives the sound — an exact match with 秣's reading.

example.hanzi: 军队正在秣马厉兵,准备战斗。
example.pinyin: Jūnduì zhèngzài mòmǎ lìbīng, zhǔnbèi zhàndòu.
example.english: The army is feeding the horses and sharpening the weapons, preparing for battle.
example.fact: 秣马厉兵 ('feed the horses, sharpen the weapons') is a common four-character idiom meaning to make thorough preparations for a battle or major undertaking.

meanings: a long day. bright. extended. clear
etymologyHint: A long 永 day 日; 永 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 日 (sun) — 昶 combines with 永 to suggest a long, bright day.
永 (yǒng, 'eternal, long') — though traditionally said to hint at the sound, 永's reading yǒng no longer resembles 昶's chǎng.

example.hanzi: “昶”常用于人名,寓意光明长久。
example.pinyin: “Chǎng” cháng yòng yú rénmíng, yùyì guāngmíng chángjiǔ.
example.english: 'Chang' is often used in personal names, symbolizing lasting brightness.
example.fact: 昶 combines 日 (sun) and 永 (long, eternal) to suggest a long, bright day; today it survives almost entirely as a character chosen for personal given names for its auspicious meaning.

components.note: 禾 (grain) — 種 relates to planting and seeds.
重 (zhòng) is close to the sound of 種 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.pinyin: “Zhǒng” shì “zhǒng” de fántǐzì.
example.english: 'Zhong' (種) is the traditional form of 'zhong' (种).
example.fact: 種/种 (zhǒng/zhòng) is common enough in modern Chinese — in words like 种子 (zhǒngzi, 'seed') and 种类 (zhǒnglèi, 'type') — that it ranks among the more frequently written characters overall.

etymologyHint: To foment 攵 rebellion 䜌

components.note: 攵 (a hand holding a stick — to strike or incite) — suggests provoking an upheaval.
䜌 (luán, tangled speech) — the image of many voices in chaos suggests instability and change.

example.hanzi: “變”是“变”的繁体字,意思是改变。
example.pinyin: “Biàn” shì “biàn” de fántǐzì, yìsi shì gǎibiàn.
example.english: 'Bian' (變) is the traditional form of 'bian' (变), meaning 'to change.'
example.fact: 變/变 (biàn, 'to change') is common enough that character simplification dramatically cut its stroke count, from 23 strokes in traditional 變 down to just 8 in simplified 变 — one of the more extreme examples of character simplification.

meanings: to rush out of a den

components.note: 穴 (a hole, den) — 窣 describes a faint sound, as of something rushing from a den.
卒 (zú) is close to the sound of 窣, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Shùyè fāchū xīsū de shēngyīn.
example.english: The leaves made a rustling sound.
example.fact: 窸窣 (xīsū) is an onomatopoeic word for a faint rustling sound, like leaves stirring in the wind or clothing brushing together.

components.note: 纟 (silk) — 绦 names a woven silk cord.
条 (tiáo) is close to the sound of 绦, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Qípáo de biān shàng xiùzhe tāozi.
example.english: The edge of the qipao is trimmed with a braided cord.
example.fact: 绦 names a woven silk braid or cord traditionally used to trim the edges of Chinese clothing, such as the qipao, adding a decorative border.

meanings: a stand for food at sacrifice
etymologyHint: A slab of meat on a chopping board 且

components.note: 仌 (two pieces, side by side) — represents slices of meat.
且 (a stand, block) — represents the chopping board itself.

example.hanzi: “人为刀俎,我为鱼肉”出自《史记》。
example.pinyin: “Rén wéi dāo zǔ, wǒ wéi yúròu” chūzì “Shǐjì”.
example.english: 'Others hold the knife and board, I am the fish and meat' comes from the Records of the Grand Historian.
example.fact: This famous line comes from the Hongmen Banquet episode in Records of the Grand Historian, where Liu Bang, at the mercy of his rival Xiang Yu, describes himself as powerless meat on someone else's chopping board (俎).

components.note: 木 (wood) — 榫 names a woodworking joint.
隼 (sǔn) gives the sound — an exact match with 榫's reading.

example.hanzi: 榫卯结构是中国传统木工技艺。
example.pinyin: Sǔnmǎo jiégòu shì Zhōngguó chuántǒng mùgōng jìyì.
example.english: Mortise-and-tenon joinery is a traditional Chinese woodworking technique.
example.fact: 榫卯 (sǔnmǎo), mortise-and-tenon joinery, lets wooden pieces interlock without nails or glue — a technique used for millennia in Chinese architecture and furniture, including parts of the Forbidden City.

components.note: 虫 (insect) — 蟪 names a kind of cicada.
惠 (huì) gives the sound — an exact match with 蟪's reading.

example.pinyin: Zhuāngzǐ shuō “huìgū bùzhī chūnqiū”.
example.english: Zhuangzi said, 'The summer cicada does not know the seasons.'
example.fact: This line from Zhuangzi's 逍遥游 ('Free and Easy Wandering') uses the short-lived summer cicada (蟪蛄), which dies before autumn, as a metaphor for how a limited lifespan limits one's perspective.

components.note: 禾 (grain) — 稗 names a weedy grain that grows among crops.
卑 (bēi) is close to the sound of 稗, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 民间流传着许多稗官野史。
example.pinyin: Mínjiān liúchuánzhe xǔduō bàiguān yěshǐ.
example.english: Many unofficial histories and folk anecdotes circulate among the people.
example.fact: 稗官野史 (bàiguān yěshǐ) refers to unofficial histories and folk anecdotes, as opposed to formal dynastic records — 稗官 originally named minor officials tasked with collecting street gossip for the court.

components.note: 言 (speech) — 謇 relates to bold, honest speaking.
宀 (mián) is close to the sound of 謇, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 屈原在《离骚》中写道“謇謇”。
example.pinyin: Qū Yuán zài “Lísāo” zhōng xiědào “jiǎnjiǎn”.
example.english: Qu Yuan wrote 'jianjian' in 'Li Sao.'
example.fact: In his poem 离骚 (Li Sao), the statesman-poet Qu Yuan uses 謇謇 (jiǎnjiǎn) to describe his own blunt, loyal remonstrance to the king — speaking honestly despite the personal risk it brought him.

components.note: 气 (gas) — 氩 names a chemical element.
亚 (yà) gives the sound — an exact match with 氩's reading.

example.hanzi: 空气中含有大约百分之一的氩气。
example.pinyin: Kōngqì zhōng hányǒu dàyuē bǎi fēn zhī yī de yàqì.
example.english: The air contains about one percent argon.
example.fact: Argon makes up about 1% of Earth's atmosphere, making it by far the most abundant noble gas in the air we breathe — it's also used inside incandescent light bulbs to keep the hot filament from oxidizing.

example.pinyin: “Lèi” shì “lèi” de fántǐzì.
example.english: 'Lei' (類) is the traditional form of 'lei' (类).
example.fact: 類/类 (lèi, 'kind, category') appears in common words like 人类 (rénlèi, 'humankind') and 分类 (fēnlèi, 'to classify'); the traditional form combines 米, 犬, and 頁, while the simplified 类 keeps only a reduced version of the left-hand side.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 锴 names high-quality iron.
皆 (jiē) no longer closely resembles 锴's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: “锴”常用作男孩的名字,意思是精铁。
example.pinyin: “Kǎi” cháng yòngzuò nánhái de míngzi, yìsi shì jīngtiě.
example.english: 'Kai' is often used as a name for boys, meaning 'fine iron.'
example.fact: 锴 (kǎi) literally means high-quality iron; because of this strong, positive meaning, it's a popular character in Chinese given names, especially for boys.

meanings: used in 齟齬|龃龉[ju3 yu3]

components.note: 齿 (teeth) — 龉 describes uneven teeth.
吾 (wú) is close to the sound of 龉, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 两人因为意见不合而产生龃龉。
example.pinyin: Liǎng rén yīnwèi yìjiàn bùhé ér chǎnshēng jǔyǔ.
example.english: The two had a falling-out because their opinions didn't match.
example.fact: 龃龉 (jǔyǔ) literally describes teeth that don't fit together properly, and is used metaphorically for people or ideas that clash and fail to mesh smoothly.

components.note: 火 (fire, linked to carbon and combustion) — hydrocarbons are combustible, carbon-based molecules.

example.hanzi: 汽油是多种烃的混合物。
example.pinyin: Qìyóu shì duō zhǒng tīng de hùnhéwù.
example.english: Gasoline is a mixture of various hydrocarbons.
example.fact: 烃 (tīng) is the general Chinese scientific term for 'hydrocarbon' — organic compounds made only of hydrogen and carbon atoms, including fuels like methane, propane, and the components of gasoline.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 俣 describes a person of impressive size.
吴 (wú) is close to the sound of 俣, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 古文用“俣俣”形容人身材魁梧。
example.pinyin: Gǔwén yòng “yǔyǔ” xíngróng rén shēncái kuíwú.
example.english: Classical texts use 'yuyu' to describe someone of imposing stature.
example.fact: 俣俣 (yǔyǔ) is a reduplicated term found in classical Chinese poetry, used to describe someone of grand, imposing stature — today 俣 survives mainly as a character chosen for personal given names.

meanings: dialectal or obsolete equivalent of 媽|妈[ma1]

components.note: 女 (woman) — 嬷 names a woman, especially a servant or nanny.
麽 (mó) is close to the sound of 嬷, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: “Hónglóumèng” lǐ yǒu hěn duō māma.
example.english: There are many nursemaids in 'Dream of the Red Chamber.'
example.fact: In classic novels like Dream of the Red Chamber, 嬷嬷 (māma) refers to an older female servant or wet-nurse in a wealthy household — a different word from, but identically pronounced to, 妈妈 ('mom').

components.note: ⺼ (flesh) — 肱 names a part of the arm.
厷 (gōng) gives the sound — an exact match with 肱's reading.

example.pinyin: Tā shì guówáng de gǔgōng zhī chén.
example.english: He is the king's most trusted minister.
example.fact: 股肱 (gǔgōng), literally 'thigh and arm,' is a classical metaphor for a ruler's most trusted and capable ministers — the body parts that do the essential work of standing and acting.

components.note: 鸟 (bird) — 鸢 names a bird of prey.
弋 (yì) is close to the sound of 鸢, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Háizimen zài fàng zhǐyuān.
example.english: The children are flying paper kites.
example.fact: 纸鸢 (zhǐyuān), literally 'paper kite-bird,' is a classical poetic name for the flying toy kite — named after the 鸢 (black kite), a real bird of prey whose soaring flight the toy imitates.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — 笫 originally named the bamboo slats forming a bed's frame.

example.pinyin: “Chuángzǐ” zhǐ de shì chuángpù.
example.english: 'Chuangzi' refers to a bed.
example.fact: 笫 originally named the bamboo slats of a bed frame; the compound 床笫 (chuángzǐ) is a literary term for the marital bed, used in the discreet phrase 床笫之私 for private matters between spouses.

meanings: a swelling of the lymph nodes

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — 痤 names a skin condition.
坐 (zuò) is close to the sound of 痤, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Qīngchūnqī róngyì zhǎng cuóchuāng.
example.english: Acne easily appears during puberty.
example.fact: 痤疮 (cuóchuāng) is the standard Chinese medical term for acne, a skin condition caused by clogged hair follicles that is especially common during puberty due to hormonal changes.

etymologyHint: The shaded side of a hill 阝; 侌 provides the pronunciation

components.note: 阝 (here the 阜 radical, 'mound, hill') — 陰 originally described the shaded, north-facing side of a hill.
侌 (yīn, clouds gathering) — closely matches 陰's own reading and depicts overcast, shaded weather.

example.hanzi: 陰陽是中国哲学的核心概念。
example.pinyin: Yīnyáng shì Zhōngguó zhéxué de héxīn gàiniàn.
example.english: Yin-yang is a core concept in Chinese philosophy.
example.fact: 陰/阴 pairs with 阳 (yang) to form 阴阳 (yin-yang), the foundational concept in Chinese philosophy describing complementary opposites such as dark and light, or passive and active forces — central to Daoism and traditional Chinese medicine.

etymologyHint: A green 艹 river 河; 河 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 艹 (grass, plant) — pairs with 河 to suggest a green river landscape.
河 (hé) matches 菏's reading exactly, and depicts a river, appropriate for this river's name.

example.pinyin: Hézé bèi chēng wéi “mǔdān zhī xiāng”.
example.english: Heze is called 'the hometown of peonies.'
example.fact: 菏泽, a city in Shandong province, is renowned as 'the hometown of peonies' (牡丹之乡), cultivating some of the most famous peony gardens in China.

components.note: 艹 (plant) — 莆 names a legendary tree.
甫 (fǔ) is close to the sound of 莆, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 莆田是妈祖信仰的发源地。
example.pinyin: Pútián shì Māzǔ xìnyǎng de fāyuándì.
example.english: Putian is the birthplace of Mazu worship.
example.fact: 莆田 (Putian), a city in Fujian province, is the birthplace of Mazu (妈祖) worship — a sea goddess still revered by many Chinese communities and overseas Chinese, especially in coastal regions.

meanings: the roots are used for various purposes
Acronym for the Chinese Elder tree 菫草

components.note: 艹 (plant) — 芨 names a medicinal plant.
及 (jí) is close to the sound of 芨 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.pinyin: Báijí shì yì zhǒng zhōngyào cái.
example.english: Baiji is a type of traditional Chinese medicinal herb.
example.fact: 白芨 (báijí), whose name contains 芨, is a flowering orchid plant whose tubers have long been used in traditional Chinese medicine, particularly for treating wounds.

meanings: classifier for songs or ci poems

components.note: 门 (gate) — 阕 originally meant to close a gate, and by extension to end or finish.
癸 (guǐ) no longer closely resembles 阕's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.pinyin: Zhè shǒu cí gòngyǒu liǎng què.
example.english: This ci-poem has two stanzas.
example.fact: 阕 is the classical measure word for a stanza of a ci-poem (词) — many famous Song-dynasty ci poems are structured in exactly two 阕, an upper and lower stanza.

components.note: 石 (stone) — 砣 names a stone or metal weight.
它 (tā) is close to the sound of 砣, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 秤砣虽小,却能称起千斤重物。
example.pinyin: Chèngtuó suī xiǎo, què néng chēng qǐ qiānjīn zhòngwù.
example.english: Though small, a steelyard weight can balance objects weighing a thousand jin.
example.fact: 秤砣 (chèngtuó), the sliding counterweight on a traditional Chinese steelyard balance scale, needs to be only a small, dense weight to balance far heavier goods on the other end.

components.note: 石 (stone) — grit in food feels like tiny bits of stone.
参 (cān) is close to the sound of 碜, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 这件衣服看起来太寒碜了。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn yīfu kànqǐlái tài hánchen le.
example.english: This piece of clothing looks too shabby.
example.fact: 碜 appears in the everyday colloquial word 寒碜 (hánchen), meaning shabby, embarrassing, or unpresentable — often used to describe clothes, a low-budget event, or a disappointing outcome.

components.note: 鼠 (rat, rodent) — 鼹 names a burrowing rodent.
晏 (yàn) is close to the sound of 鼹 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.hanzi: 鼹鼠大部分时间生活在地下。
example.pinyin: Yǎnshǔ dàbùfen shíjiān shēnghuó zài dìxià.
example.english: Moles spend most of their time living underground.
example.fact: 鼹鼠 (yǎnshǔ), moles, spend nearly their whole lives underground and have very small, weak eyes, since eyesight isn't very useful in constant darkness.

etymologyHint: An old man with long hair and a cane

example.pinyin: “Zhǎng” shì “zhǎng” de fántǐzì.
example.english: 'Zhang' (長) is the traditional form of 'zhang' (长).
example.fact: 長/长 (zhǎng/cháng) is one of the most drastically simplified common characters — the traditional 長, drawn to depict an old man with long flowing hair and a cane, was reduced to just a few strokes in simplified 长.

components.note: 犬 (dog) — its link to 猷's meaning 'plan, scheme' is not transparent; the character survives today mainly in literary compounds.
酋 (qiú) no longer closely resembles 猷's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.pinyin: Tā yǒu hóngyóu dàlüè.
example.english: He has grand plans and great strategy.
example.fact: 猷 is a literary word for 'plan, scheme,' most often seen today in given names or in classical compounds like 宏猷 ('grand plan') describing ambitious, far-sighted strategy.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — 竽 names an ancient bamboo wind instrument.
于 (yú) gives the sound — an exact match with 竽's reading.

example.hanzi: “滥竽充数”是一个著名的成语故事。
example.pinyin: “Lànyú chōngshù” shì yí gè zhùmíng de chéngyǔ gùshi.
example.english: 'Passing off as a yu player to make up numbers' is a famous idiom story.
example.fact: The idiom 滥竽充数 tells of an untalented musician who hid among 300 skilled 竽 players in the King of Qi's orchestra, exposed only when the king later demanded solo performances — it now describes anyone passing off as competent by hiding within a group.

components.note: 舟 (boat) — 舸 names a large boat.
可 (kě) is close to the sound of 舸, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 毛泽东的词中有“百舸争流”。
example.pinyin: Máo Zédōng de cí zhōng yǒu “bǎi gě zhēng liú”.
example.english: Mao Zedong's poem contains the phrase 'a hundred boats vie on the current.'
example.fact: 百舸争流 ('a hundred barges vie on the current') is a line from Mao Zedong's 1925 poem 《沁园春·长沙》, describing the busy river traffic of Changsha — one of his most widely studied poems in Chinese schools.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 诓 means to deceive with words.
匡 (kuāng) gives the sound — an exact match with 诓's reading.

example.pinyin: Piànzi kuāngpiàn le hěn duō lǎorén.
example.english: The swindler deceived many elderly people.
example.fact: 诓骗 (kuāngpiàn) is a common word for deceiving or swindling someone, frequently seen in Chinese news reports warning about scams targeting vulnerable groups such as the elderly.

etymologyHint: A metal 金 cutting tool 斩; 斩 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 金 (metal) — 錾 names a metal engraving tool.
斩 (zhǎn, 'to cut') — a chisel cuts into metal; its reading is only loosely close to 錾's zàn.

example.hanzi: 银器上的花纹是錾刻出来的。
example.pinyin: Yínqì shàng de huāwén shì zànkè chūlái de.
example.english: The patterns on the silverware were chiseled and engraved.
example.fact: 錾刻 (zànkè) is a traditional Chinese metalworking technique using a chisel to hammer intricate patterns directly into gold, silver, or copper — still used today in fine jewelry and decorative metalwork.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 淬 means to plunge hot metal into water to harden it.
卒 (zú) is close to the sound of 淬, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 铁匠把烧红的刀刃淬火。
example.pinyin: Tiějiang bǎ shāo hóng de dāorèn cuìhuǒ.
example.english: The blacksmith quenched the red-hot blade.
example.fact: 淬火 (cuìhuǒ), quenching, is the metallurgical process of rapidly cooling red-hot metal in water or oil to harden it — an essential step in both traditional swordmaking and modern steel manufacturing.

components.note: 阝 (here the 阜 radical, 'mound, hill') — 隗 originally described something high or lofty.
鬼 (guǐ) is close to the sound of 隗, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: “Xiān cóng Kuí shǐ” shì yí gè lìshǐ diǎngù.
example.english: 'Start with Kui first' is a historical anecdote.
example.fact: 先从隗始 ('start with Kui first') comes from a Warring States-era story about attracting talented advisers: by rewarding even a modest candidate first, a ruler proves his sincerity, encouraging truly great talents to come forward.

meanings: to do one's duty as a younger brother
etymologyHint: Fraternal 弟 respect 忄; 弟 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 悌 describes an inner feeling of respect toward one's elder siblings.
弟 (dì, 'younger brother') — 悌 is specifically the respect owed between siblings; its reading only loosely resembles 悌's tì.

example.hanzi: 孝悌是儒家提倡的美德。
example.pinyin: Xiàotì shì Rújiā tíchàng de měidé.
example.english: Filial piety and brotherly respect are virtues advocated by Confucianism.
example.fact: 孝悌 (xiàotì), filial piety toward parents combined with respect toward elder siblings, is one of the core virtues in Confucian ethics, emphasized throughout classical texts like the Analects.

meanings: to be a mistress or lover
etymologyHint: An affair 并 with a woman 女; 并 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 女 (woman) — 姘 describes an illicit relationship.
并 (bìng, 'together, joined') — suggests two people joined together outside of marriage; its reading only loosely resembles 姘's pīn.

example.pinyin: Fǎlǜ bù chéngrèn pīnjū guānxì.
example.english: The law does not recognize such cohabitation relationships.
example.fact: 姘 is a formal or legal term for an illicit romantic relationship outside of marriage, as in 姘居 (pīnjū) — a word encountered mainly in legal or literary contexts rather than everyday speech.

components.note: 木 (tree) — 槭 names the maple tree.
戚 (qī) gives the sound — an exact match with 槭's reading.

example.hanzi: 秋天槭树的叶子变红了。
example.pinyin: Qiūtiān qī shù de yèzi biàn hóng le.
example.english: In autumn, the maple tree's leaves turn red.
example.fact: 槭 is a formal, scientific name for maple trees (genus Acer), while everyday Chinese usually uses the more common word 枫 for maple, especially its famous red autumn leaves.

components.note: 辶 (to walk, move) — 邈 describes something far off in distance.
貌 (mào) is close to the sound of 邈, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 那段历史已经邈远难寻。
example.pinyin: Nà duàn lìshǐ yǐjīng miǎoyuǎn nánxún.
example.english: That period of history is now distant and hard to trace.
example.fact: 邈 is a literary word meaning far or distant in space or time, often paired with 远 in 邈远 to describe something so far removed it feels almost impossible to reach or recall.

components.note: 女 (woman) — 婕 is used only as part of a woman's title or name.
疌 (an ancient component rarely used on its own) no longer resembles 婕's modern reading jié — the connection has been lost over time.

example.hanzi: 班婕妤是汉代著名的才女。
example.pinyin: Bān Jiéyú shì Hàndài zhùmíng de cáinǚ.
example.english: Ban Jieyu was a famous talented woman of the Han dynasty.
example.fact: 婕妤 (jiéyú) was a rank of imperial consort in the Han-dynasty court; its most famous holder, the poet Ban Jieyu, was celebrated for her literary talent and later became a recurring figure in Chinese poetry and opera.

components.note: 欠 (to exhale, related to breathing) — historically groups 歙 among characters relating to breath or air, though 歙 survives today mainly as a place name.
翕 (xī) no longer closely resembles 歙's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.pinyin: Shèxiàn yǐ shèyàn wénmíng.
example.english: Shexian is famous for its inkstones.
example.fact: 歙砚 (shèyàn), produced in Shexian county of Anhui province, is one of the Four Famous Inkstones of China, prized by calligraphers for centuries alongside the equally famous Duan inkstone.

components.note: 禾 (grain) — 稹 originally described grain packed densely together.
真 (zhēn) is close to the sound of 稹 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.pinyin: Yuán Zhěn shì Tángdài zhùmíng shīrén.
example.english: Yuan Zhen was a famous Tang-dynasty poet.
example.fact: 元稹 (Yuan Zhen) was a celebrated Tang-dynasty poet and close friend of the more famous Bai Juyi; together they pioneered the 'New Yuefu' poetry movement advocating socially engaged verse.

etymologyHint: To approach 就 in one leap 足; 足 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 足 (foot) — 蹴 means to kick.
就 (jiù, 'to approach, accomplish') — paired with 足, suggests reaching a goal in a single leap; its reading no longer resembles 蹴's cù.

example.hanzi: 蹴鞠是中国古代的足球运动。
example.pinyin: Cùjū shì Zhōngguó gǔdài de zúqiú yùndòng.
example.english: Cuju was an ancient Chinese form of football.
example.fact: 蹴鞠 (cùjū), an ancient Chinese ball game played by kicking a leather ball into a net, dates back over 2,000 years to the Han dynasty and is recognized as one of the earliest known forms of football.

components.note: 石 (mineral) — 砒 names a mineral-derived poison.
比 (bǐ) is close to the sound of 砒, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 砒霜是一种含砒元素的毒药。
example.pinyin: Pīshuāng shì yì zhǒng hán pī yuánsù de dúyào.
example.english: Arsenic trioxide is a poison containing the element arsenic.
example.fact: 砒霜 (pīshuāng, arsenic trioxide) was historically one of the most infamous poisons in Chinese history and literature, appearing in classical novels such as Water Margin as the poison used in a notorious plot.

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — 痈 names a skin infection.
用 (yòng) is close to the sound of 痈 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.hanzi: 姑息问题就是养痈遗患。
example.pinyin: Gūxī wèntí jiùshì yǎngyōng yíhuàn.
example.english: Tolerating a problem is like nurturing a boil that will cause future trouble.
example.fact: The idiom 养痈遗患 ('nurturing an abscess leaves future trouble') warns that failing to address a small problem promptly, like an untreated skin infection, only lets it grow into something much worse.

etymologyHint: A metal 钅 still 留; 留 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 镏 relates to metal, both in chemistry and in jewelry.
留 (liú) matches 镏's reading exactly, and means 'to remain, stay' — fitting for both distilled liquid left behind and a ring kept on the finger.

example.pinyin: Nǎinai yǒu yí gè jīn liùzi.
example.english: Grandma has a gold ring.
example.fact: In northern Chinese dialects, 镏子 (liùzi) is a colloquial word for a ring, especially a gold one — a different, everyday sense from 镏's more technical uses in chemistry and distillation.

components.note: 羊 (sheep) — 羯 names a castrated ram.
曷 (hé) no longer closely resembles 羯's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.pinyin: Jiézú shì Wǔhú zhī yī.
example.english: The Jie people were one of the Five Barbarian groups.
example.fact: The 羯 (Jie) people were one of the 'Five Barbarians' (五胡) who established kingdoms in northern China during its 4th-century political fragmentation — their leader Shi Le founded the Later Zhao dynasty.

etymologyHint: A pig drawn on its side

example.hanzi: “豕”是汉字部首之一,意思是猪。
example.pinyin: “Shǐ” shì Hànzì bùshǒu zhī yī, yìsi shì zhū.
example.english: 'Shi' is one of the Chinese character radicals, meaning 'pig.'
example.fact: 豕 depicts a pig viewed from the side and serves as Kangxi radical 152 — one of the 214 traditional radicals used to organize entries in Chinese dictionaries.

components.note: 鱼 (fish) — 鲂 names a freshwater fish.
方 (fāng) is close to the sound of 鲂 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.hanzi: 鲂鱼自古就是人们喜爱的食用鱼。
example.pinyin: Fángyú zìgǔ jiùshì rénmen xǐ'ài de shíyòng yú.
example.english: Bream has been a favorite food fish among people since ancient times.
example.fact: 鲂 (bream) is mentioned as a prized food fish as far back as the Book of Songs (诗经), China's oldest poetry collection, showing that freshwater fish have been part of Chinese cuisine for millennia.

components.note: 艹 (plant) — 蓖 names the castor-oil plant.
比 (bǐ) is close to the sound of 蓖 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.hanzi: 蓖麻油可以用来做润滑剂。
example.pinyin: Bìmáyóu kěyǐ yòng lái zuò rùnhuájì.
example.english: Castor oil can be used to make lubricant.
example.fact: 蓖麻油 (bìmáyóu, castor oil), pressed from castor beans, has been used for centuries both as a traditional medicine ingredient and, more recently, as an industrial lubricant and biodiesel ingredient.

components.note: 匚 (a box, container) — 匦 names a small box.
轨 (guǐ) gives the sound — an exact match with 匦's reading.

example.hanzi: 唐朝武则天设立了铜匦,供百姓上书。
example.pinyin: Tángcháo Wǔ Zétiān shèlì le tóngguǐ, gōng bǎixìng shàngshū.
example.english: The Tang-dynasty Empress Wu Zetian established bronze boxes for common people to submit petitions.
example.fact: Empress Wu Zetian of the Tang dynasty set up bronze petition boxes (铜匦) with separate slots for different kinds of complaints and suggestions — an early system letting ordinary citizens communicate directly with the court.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — 笤 names a broom traditionally made from bamboo or bound twigs.
召 (zhào) no longer closely resembles 笤's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.pinyin: Tā yòng tiáozhou dǎsǎo dìmiàn.
example.english: She swept the floor with a broom.
example.fact: 笤帚 (tiáozhou) is the everyday Chinese word for a small hand broom, traditionally made from bound sorghum or bamboo twigs.

meanings: used in 崢嶸|峥嵘[zheng1 rong2]

components.note: 山 (mountain) — 峥 describes something towering and lofty.
争 (zhēng) gives the sound — an exact match with 峥's reading.

example.pinyin: Nà shì yí duàn zhēngróng suìyuè.
example.english: Those were extraordinary, momentous years.
example.fact: 峥嵘岁月 (zhēngróng suìyuè), literally 'towering years,' is a common phrase for an extraordinary, momentous period of time — often used in China to describe the revolutionary era of the early 20th century.

components.note: 彳 (a step, related to walking) — 徭 relates to compulsory labor service performed away from home.
䍃 (yáo) gives the sound — an exact match with 徭's reading.

example.pinyin: Qíncháo de yáoyì fēicháng fánzhòng.
example.english: Corvee labor during the Qin dynasty was extremely heavy.
example.fact: 徭役 (yáoyì), the corvee labor system, required commoners in imperial China to perform unpaid work for the state, such as building the Great Wall or digging canals — the heavy burden of Qin-dynasty corvee labor is often cited as a cause of the unrest that helped topple the dynasty.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 浃 means to be thoroughly soaked.
夹 (jiā) gives the sound — an exact match with 浃's reading.

example.pinyin: Tā pǎo wán bù hòu hànliú jiābèi.
example.english: After running, he was drenched in sweat.
example.fact: 汗流浃背 (hànliú jiābèi), 'sweat drenching the back,' is a common idiom for being soaked in sweat from hard exertion, extreme heat, or intense nervousness.

components.note: 火 (fire) — 烊 originally meant to melt metal with heat.
羊 (yáng) gives the sound — an exact match with 烊's reading.
