example.pinyin: Shāngdiàn wǎnshàng shí diǎn dǎyáng.
example.english: The shop closes at ten at night.
example.fact: 打烊 (dǎyáng), 'to close up shop,' is common in Shanghainese-influenced Mandarin and Taiwanese Mandarin; 烊 originally meant to melt metal, since a shop closing for the night was likened to metal being melted down at day's end.

components.note: 衤 (cloth) — 補 means to mend clothing.
甫 (fǔ) is close to the sound of 補, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: “Bǔ” shì “bǔ” de fántǐzì.
example.english: 'Bu' (補) is the traditional form of 'bu' (补).
example.fact: 補/补 (bǔ, 'to mend, repair, replenish') appears in common words like 补充 (bǔchōng, 'to supplement') and 修补 (xiūbǔ, 'to repair') — the simplified 补 replaces the traditional phonetic component 甫 with the simpler 卜.

components.note: 穴 (a hole, den) — 窸 describes a faint sound.
悉 (xī) gives the sound — an exact match with 窸's reading.

example.hanzi: 老鼠在墙角发出窸窣声。
example.pinyin: Lǎoshǔ zài qiángjiǎo fāchū xīsū shēng.
example.english: A mouse makes a rustling sound in the corner.
example.fact: 窸窣 (xīsū) is an onomatopoeic word for a faint rustling sound; unlike its partner character 窣, which can occasionally stand alone, 窸 exists only paired with 窣.

components.note: 阝 (here the 邑 radical, 'place') — 酆 names an ancient capital.
豐 (fēng) gives the sound — an exact match with 酆's reading.

example.hanzi: 酆是周文王建立的都城。
example.pinyin: Fēng shì Zhōu Wénwáng jiànlì de dūchéng.
example.english: Feng was the capital established by King Wen of Zhou.
example.fact: 酆 (also written 丰) was the capital King Wen of Zhou built near modern Xi'an before the Zhou dynasty's founding — later paired with a second capital, Hao (镐), the two together known as 丰镐.

meanings: (literary) to die by hanging or strangulation

components.note: 纟 (thread, rope) — 缢 means to hang by a rope.
益 (yì) gives the sound — an exact match with 缢's reading.

example.hanzi: 明朝末代皇帝在景山自缢。
example.pinyin: Míngcháo mòdài huángdì zài Jǐngshān zìyì.
example.english: The last emperor of the Ming dynasty hanged himself on Jingshan.
example.fact: In 1644, as rebel forces closed in on Beijing, the last Ming emperor, Chongzhen, is recorded as having ended his life on Jingshan hill behind the Forbidden City, marking the fall of the Ming dynasty.

meanings: used in 褓姆[bao3 mu3] and 褓母[bao3 mu3]
etymologyHint: A cloth 衤 used to protect 保 an infant; 保 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 衤 (cloth) — 褓 names cloth used to wrap an infant.
保 (bǎo) matches 褓's reading exactly, and means 'to protect' — fitting for cloth meant to protect a baby.

example.pinyin: Tā hái zài qiǎngbǎo zhōng.
example.english: He is still in swaddling clothes.
example.fact: 襁褓 (qiǎngbǎo), the word for swaddling clothes, is often used figuratively for very early infancy, as in 还在襁褓中 ('still in the cradle').

components.note: 虫 (insect) — 蚨 names a water beetle.
夫 (fū) gives the sound — an exact match with 蚨's reading.

example.pinyin: Gǔrén chēng qián wéi “qīngfú”.
example.english: Ancient people called money 'qingfu.'
example.fact: According to an old Chinese legend, a mother water-beetle called 青蚨 always returns to where her young are kept; from this, coins were fancifully said to always 'return' too, giving 蚨 an old slang meaning of 'money.'

components.note: 羽 (feather) — 翳 originally referred to a feathered screen used to hide behind.
殹 (yì) gives the sound — an exact match with 翳's reading.

example.pinyin: Tā de yǎnjing zhǎng le yì.
example.english: A film has grown over his eye.
example.fact: In traditional Chinese medicine, 翳 refers to a cloudy film or opacity over the eye — a concept covering what modern medicine describes as conditions like corneal scarring or cataracts.

components.note: 走 (to walk) — 趔 describes an unsteady, stumbling gait.
列 (liè) gives the sound — an exact match with 趔's reading.

example.pinyin: Tā bèi zhuàng de lièqie le yíxià.
example.english: He staggered after being bumped into.
example.fact: 趔趄 (lièqie) describes stumbling or staggering unsteadily, often after being bumped, pushed, or momentarily losing one's balance.

components.note: 火 (fire) — 炔 (alkyne) compounds are highly flammable.
夬 (guài) is close to the sound of 炔, but not an exact match.

example.hanzi: 他姓炔,是这里少见的姓氏。
example.pinyin: Tā xìng Guì, shì zhèlǐ shǎojiàn de xìngshì.
example.english: His surname is Gui, a rare surname around here.
example.fact: 炔, read here as the surname Guì, has an entirely different pronunciation, quē, when used in chemistry to name alkynes such as acetylene — one character serving two very different vocabularies with two different sounds.

components.note: 言 (speech, writing) — 誊 means to copy out a written text.
龹 (an ancient component rarely used on its own) no longer resembles 誊's modern reading téng — the connection has been lost over time.

example.hanzi: 请把答案誊写在答题卡上。
example.pinyin: Qǐng bǎ dá'àn téngxiě zài dátíkǎ shàng.
example.english: Please transcribe the answers onto the answer sheet.
example.fact: 誊写 (téngxiě), 'to transcribe,' is a word Chinese students hear constantly during exams, instructing them to carefully copy their draft answers onto the official answer sheet.

components.note: 臣 (minister) — its link to 赜's meaning 'profound, abstruse' is not transparent today.
责 (zé) gives the sound — an exact match with 赜's reading.

example.hanzi: 学者们探赜索隐,研究古代哲学。
example.pinyin: Xuézhěmen tànzé suǒyǐn, yánjiū gǔdài zhéxué.
example.english: Scholars probe the profound and seek out the hidden, studying ancient philosophy.
example.fact: 探赜索隐 ('to probe the profound and search out the hidden') comes from the ancient classic Book of Changes (《易经》), describing the deep, painstaking inquiry needed to understand profound truths.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 仃 describes a person who is alone.
丁 (dīng) gives the sound — an exact match with 仃's reading.

example.hanzi: 老人孤苦伶仃地生活着。
example.pinyin: Lǎorén gūkǔ língdīng de shēnghuózhe.
example.english: The elderly person lives all alone, without support.
example.fact: 孤苦伶仃 (gūkǔ língdīng) is a common idiom describing someone utterly alone and without family or support — 仃 exists in modern Chinese almost only inside this phrase and its shorter form 伶仃.

components.note: 力 (strength, effort) — 勖 means to urge someone to greater effort.
冒 (mào) no longer closely resembles 勖's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 老师勖勉学生努力学习。
example.pinyin: Lǎoshī xùmiǎn xuésheng nǔlì xuéxí.
example.english: The teacher encourages students to study hard.
example.fact: 勖 is a classical, formal word meaning to encourage or exhort someone to effort; today it survives mainly in the literary compound 勖勉 (xùmiǎn, 'to encourage') and as a character occasionally chosen for given names.

components.note: 艹 (grass) — 葺 originally meant to thatch a roof with plant material.
咠 (qì) gives the sound — an exact match with 葺's reading.

example.pinyin: Zhè zuò gǔmiào zhèngzài xiūqì.
example.english: This ancient temple is being renovated.
example.fact: 修葺 (xiūqì) is the formal word for renovating or repairing a building, frequently seen in Chinese news reports about restoring historic temples, palaces, and monuments.

etymologyHint: An immature 幼 insect 虫; 幼 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 虫 (insect) — 蚴 names the larval stage of a parasitic worm.
幼 (yòu) matches 蚴's reading exactly, and means 'young, immature' — precisely 蚴's meaning.

example.hanzi: 血吸虫的蚴虫会感染人体。
example.pinyin: Xuèxīchóng de yòuchóng huì gǎnrǎn réntǐ.
example.english: The larvae of the blood fluke can infect the human body.
example.fact: 蚴 specifically refers to a parasitic worm's larval stage, most often seen in biology and medical texts discussing parasites such as schistosomes (血吸虫).

components.note: 氵 (water) — 泷 describes river rapids.
龙 (lóng) gives the sound — an exact match with 泷's reading.

example.pinyin: Lóng shì jíliú de yìsi.
example.english: 'Long' means rapid currents.
example.fact: 泷 means river rapids in Chinese, and closely resembles the Japanese character 滝 (taki), meaning 'waterfall' — a reminder of how Chinese characters spread across East Asia and sometimes developed related but distinct meanings in each language.

meanings: used in 蠐螬|蛴螬[qi2 cao2]
used in 蝤蠐|蝤蛴[qiu2 qi2]

components.note: 虫 (insect) — 蛴 names a type of grub.
齐 (qí) gives the sound — an exact match with 蛴's reading.

example.hanzi: 《诗经》用“蝤蛴”比喻美人的脖子。
example.pinyin: “Shījīng” yòng “qiúqí” bǐyù měirén de bózi.
example.english: The Book of Songs uses 'qiuqi' to describe a beautiful woman's neck.
example.fact: In the Book of Songs (诗经), the poem 硕人 compares a beauty's smooth white neck to 蝤蛴, the plump white grub of a longhorn beetle — a simile that might seem strange to modern readers but was a classical compliment.

components.note: 糹 (silk) — 結 means to tie or knot, as with thread.
吉 (jí) is close to the sound of 結, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: “Jié” shì “jié” de fántǐzì.
example.english: 'Jie' (結) is the traditional form of 'jie' (结).
example.fact: 結/结 (jié, 'knot, to tie') is common in words like 结婚 (jiéhūn, 'to marry') and 结束 (jiéshù, 'to end') — the simplified form replaces the traditional silk radical 糹 with the shorter 纟.

components.note: 女 (woman) — 媸 describes an unattractive woman.
蚩 (chī) gives the sound — an exact match with 媸's reading.

example.pinyin: Yánchī bùnéng zhǐ kàn wàibiǎo.
example.english: Beauty and ugliness cannot be judged by appearance alone.
example.fact: 媸 appears mainly in the classical pairing 妍媸 (yánchī, 'beautiful and ugly'), used in literary Chinese to discuss discerning true quality or character rather than surface appearance.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 俳 names a kind of performer.
非 (fēi) no longer closely resembles 俳's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 俳句是日本的一种短诗。
example.pinyin: Páijù shì Rìběn de yì zhǒng duǎnshī.
example.english: Haiku is a form of short Japanese poetry.
example.fact: 俳句 (páijù), the Chinese name for the Japanese haiku, borrows the character 俳, which in classical Chinese originally meant a jester, clown, or comic performer.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 诖 relates to being misled by words.
圭 (guī) is close to the sound of 诖, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Tā yīn guàwù ér shòudào qiānlián.
example.english: He was implicated after being misled into another's fault.
example.fact: 诖误 (guàwù) is an archaic literary term meaning to be misled into wrongdoing or implicated in someone else's fault — a word now confined to classical texts and legal history.

components.note: 艹 (a weed, plant) — 茑 names a climbing plant.
鸟 (niǎo) gives the sound — an exact match with 茑's reading.

example.pinyin: Niǎoluó shì yì zhǒng pānpá zhíwù.
example.english: Cypress vine is a climbing plant.
example.fact: 茑萝 (niǎoluó, cypress vine) is a delicate climbing garden flower with star-shaped red or white blooms, popular in Chinese gardens for covering trellises and fences.

components.note: 辶 (to walk, move) — 逡 means to retreat or hold back.
夋 (an ancient component rarely used on its own) no longer resembles 逡's modern reading qūn — the connection has been lost over time.

example.hanzi: 他逡巡不前,不敢做决定。
example.pinyin: Tā qūnxún bùqián, bù gǎn zuò juédìng.
example.english: He hesitated and held back, not daring to make a decision.
example.fact: 逡巡 (qūnxún) describes hesitant retreat or reluctance to move forward — a literary word for hanging back out of caution or fear.

meanings: used in 孱頭|孱头[can4 tou5]
etymologyHint: Weak 孨 in body 尸

components.note: 尸 (body) — 孱 describes physical frailty.
孨 (weak, delicate) — reinforces the sense of frailty in 孱.

example.hanzi: 别叫他孱头,他其实很勇敢。
example.pinyin: Bié jiào tā càntou, tā qíshí hěn yǒnggǎn.
example.english: Don't call him a weakling, he's actually very brave.
example.fact: 孱头 (càntou) is colloquial Mandarin slang, especially in Beijing dialect, for a timid, ineffectual person — a 'weakling' — while the more literary reading chán appears in the formal word 孱弱 ('frail, weak').

components.note: 石 (stone) — 砦 names a stone or earthen fortification.
此 (cǐ) no longer closely resembles 砦's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.pinyin: Gǔdài shān shàng cháng jiàn yǒu zhài.
example.english: Ancient mountains often had stockades built on them.
example.fact: 砦 is a variant of 寨 (zhài), meaning a stockade or fortified outpost — such mountain strongholds feature prominently in classical novels like Water Margin, where outlaws gather in fortified mountain hideouts.

meanings: to clear streets when emperor tours

components.note: 足 (foot) — 跸 relates to halting foot traffic on a road.
毕 (bì) gives the sound — an exact match with 跸's reading.

example.hanzi: 皇帝出行时,侍卫要清道跸路。
example.pinyin: Huángdì chūxíng shí, shìwèi yào qīng dào bì lù.
example.english: When the emperor traveled, guards had to clear the road.
example.fact: 跸 refers specifically to clearing the road and halting traffic for an emperor's procession — the historical term 驻跸 named the place where the imperial entourage stopped to rest during a journey.

components.note: 礻 (spirit, ritual) — 祜 names a blessing from the heavens.
古 (gǔ) is close to the sound of 祜, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: “Hù” cháng yòng yú zhùfú xìng de míngzi.
example.english: 'Hu' is often used in names with blessing connotations.
example.fact: 祜 means divine blessing or prosperity and is used almost exclusively today as a character in given names, chosen for its auspicious, hopeful meaning.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 伉 relates to a paired person, a spouse.
亢 (kàng) gives the sound — an exact match with 伉's reading.

example.hanzi: 他们是令人羡慕的伉俪。
example.pinyin: Tāmen shì lìng rén xiànmù de kànglì.
example.english: They are an enviable married couple.
example.fact: 伉俪 (kànglì) is a formal, respectful term for a married couple, commonly used in wedding toasts, obituaries, and formal writing in place of the more casual 夫妻.

etymologyHint: A noxious 臭 liquid 氵; 臭 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 氵 (water, liquid) — 溴 is the only nonmetal element that is liquid at room temperature.
臭 (here read xiù, 'smell') — matches 溴's reading exactly, and names its famously strong odor.

example.hanzi: 溴是室温下唯一的液态非金属元素。
example.pinyin: Xiù shì shìwēn xià wéiyī de yètài fēijīnshǔ yuánsù.
example.english: Bromine is the only nonmetal element that is liquid at room temperature.
example.fact: Bromine is one of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature (the other is the metal mercury); its name comes from the Greek word for 'stench,' reflecting its strong, unpleasant smell.

components.note: 彳 (a step, related to walking) — 屐 names a kind of footwear.
尸 (shī) is close to the sound of 屐, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Gǔrén cháng chuān mùjī pá shān.
example.english: Ancient people often wore wooden clogs to climb mountains.
example.fact: 木屐 (wooden clogs) have a long history in China that predates their strong modern association with Japanese footwear — Tang-dynasty poets are recorded wearing similar wooden clogs for hiking in the mountains.

etymologyHint: A particularly fierce 焱 storm 风

components.note: 风 (wind) — 飚 names a fierce storm.
焱 (yàn, blazing flames) — paired with 风, suggests a wind as fierce and consuming as fire.

example.pinyin: Fángjià zuìjìn biāoshēng.
example.english: Housing prices have recently skyrocketed.
example.fact: 飙 (of which 飚 is a variant) combines 风 (wind) with 焱 (blazing flames) to depict a fierce whirlwind; today it commonly appears in modern words like 飙升 (biāoshēng, 'to skyrocket') and 飙车 (biāochē, 'to speed, street race').

meanings: used in 蛞螻|蛞蝼[kuo4 lou2]

components.note: 虫 (insect, small creature) — 蛞 names a small mollusk.
舌 (shé) no longer closely resembles 蛞's sound — the reading has drifted apart over time, though it's traditionally analyzed as the phonetic component.

example.hanzi: 蛞蝓是没有壳的软体动物。
example.pinyin: Kuòyú shì méiyǒu ké de ruǎntǐ dòngwù.
example.english: Slugs are mollusks without shells.
example.fact: 蛞蝓 (kuòyú) is the standard Chinese zoological term for a slug — essentially a snail that has lost its shell over the course of evolution.

components.note: 釒 (metal) — 鏡 was originally a polished bronze disc.
竟 (jìng) gives the sound — an exact match with 鏡's reading.

example.hanzi: “鏡”是“镜”的繁体字,意思是镜子。
example.pinyin: “Jìng” shì “jìng” de fántǐzì, yìsi shì jìngzi.
example.english: 'Jing' (鏡) is the traditional form of 'jing' (镜), meaning 'mirror.'
example.fact: 鏡/镜 (jìng, 'mirror') appears in 眼镜 (yǎnjìng, 'eyeglasses') and 望远镜 (wàngyuǎnjìng, 'telescope') — the traditional form keeps the full 金 (metal) radical, reflecting mirrors' ancient origin as polished bronze discs.

etymologyHint: To bear 扌 on the shoulders 肩; 肩 also provides the pronunciation

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 掮 means to carry something on the shoulder.
肩 (jiān, 'shoulder') — names exactly where the load is carried; its reading is only loosely close to 掮's qián.

example.pinyin: Tā shì yí gè fángdìchǎn qiánkè.
example.english: He is a real estate broker.
example.fact: 掮客 (qiánkè), literally 'one who carries on the shoulder,' is a Chinese word for a broker or deal-making middleman — the image of physically carrying a burden extended to carrying deals between two parties.

components.note: 山 (mountain) — 崆 names a mountain.
空 (kōng) gives the sound — an exact match with 崆's reading.

example.hanzi: 崆峒山是著名的道教圣地。
example.pinyin: Kōngtóng Shān shì zhùmíng de Dàojiào shèngdì.
example.english: Mount Kongtong is a famous Daoist sacred site.
example.fact: 崆峒山, in Gansu province, is a famous Daoist sacred mountain; according to legend recorded in the Zhuangzi, the mythical Yellow Emperor traveled there to seek teachings on the Dao from the sage Guangchengzi.

components.note: 广 (a shelter, building) — 庾 names a granary building.
臾 (yú) is close to the sound of 庾 — the same syllable, just a different tone.

example.hanzi: 庾信是南北朝时期的著名文学家。
example.pinyin: Yǔ Xìn shì Nánběicháo shíqī de zhùmíng wénxuéjiā.
example.english: Yu Xin was a famous writer of the Northern and Southern Dynasties period.
example.fact: 庾信 (Yu Xin) was one of the most celebrated poets and essayists of the Northern and Southern Dynasties period, renowned for blending the ornate southern literary style with the more austere northern one after being forced to serve at a northern court.

components.note: 木 (wood) — 橛 names a wooden stake.
厥 (jué) gives the sound — an exact match with 橛's reading.

example.pinyin: Tā bǎ shéngzi bǎng zài juézi shàng.
example.english: He tied the rope to the stake.
example.fact: 橛 names a wooden stake or post driven into the ground, traditionally used for tethering animals or marking a boundary.

components.note: 石 (rock) — 矸 names a type of rock.
干 (gān) gives the sound — an exact match with 矸's reading.

example.hanzi: 煤矸石是采煤后剩下的废石。
example.pinyin: Méigānshí shì cǎi méi hòu shèngxià de fèishí.
example.english: Coal gangue is the waste rock left over after coal mining.
example.fact: 煤矸石 (méigānshí, coal gangue) is the waste rock separated from coal during mining and processing — one of the largest industrial solid wastes in coal-mining regions, now increasingly recycled into building materials.

components.note: 鸟 (bird) — 鸨 names a large bird.
匕 (bǐ) is close to the sound of 鸨, but not an exact match.

example.pinyin: Dàbǎo shì yì zhǒng dàxíng niǎolèi.
example.english: The great bustard is a large bird.
example.fact: 鸨 names the bustard, one of the heaviest flying birds in the world; the character separately became old slang for a brothel madam (老鸨), an unrelated meaning that arose purely from a pun on the sound.
